title: Cheapest Climb to the Top
statement:
A staircase has steps numbered 0 to n − 1. Standing on step i costs cost[i], paid once each time you land there. The top is just past the last step, at position n, and costs nothing.

You may begin on step 0 or step 1 (you pay for the step you begin on). From step i you move to i + 1 or i + 2. Return the smallest total cost to reach the top.

examples.why: Steps 0, 2, 4: 0 + 7 + 6. Always stepping to the cheaper of the next two steps goes 0, 4, 7, 6 and pays 17.
Begin on step 1 and jump two straight to the top. The last step does not have to be touched.
Steps 1, 3, 4, then a 2-jump over the 9 to the top: 4 + 1 + 0.

hints: Think about the last step you stand on before the top. It is either step n − 1 or step n − 2.
Let best(i) be the cheapest way to stand on step i, including its own cost. You got to i from i − 1 or from i − 2.
best(i) = cost[i] + min(best(i − 1), best(i − 2)), with best(0) = cost[0] and best(1) = cost[1]. The answer is min(best(n − 1), best(n − 2)). Two variables are enough.

explain.intuition:
Greedy fails here because a cheap step can lead only to expensive ones. You have to compare whole routes, and DP does that by remembering, for every step, the cheapest route that ends there.

State: best(i) = the cheapest total paid to be standing on step i, with cost[i] included. Recurrence: you arrived from i − 1 or i − 2, so best(i) = cost[i] + min(best(i − 1), best(i − 2)). You may begin on 0 or 1, so best(0) = cost[0] and best(1) = cost[1]. The top is reached by one more move from n − 1 or n − 2, so the answer is min(best(n − 1), best(n − 2)).
steps: State: best(i) = cheapest total cost to be standing on step i, paying cost[i].
Base cases: best(0) = cost[0], best(1) = cost[1], since you may begin on either.
Fill i = 2 … n − 1 keeping only the last two values.
Answer: min(best(n − 1), best(n − 2)). The top can be reached from either.
pitfalls: Returning best(n − 1). That forces you to step on the last stair; on [1, 1, 100] it answers 101 instead of 1.
Picking the cheaper of the next two steps each time. On the first example that pays 17 instead of 13.
Forcing a start on step 0. Beginning on step 1 is free to choose, and in the third example it is the only way to get 5.

solutions.title: Plain recursion
solutions.idea: best(i) from the recurrence, without caching. Every route is explored, so the time doubles roughly every step.

solutions.title: Table, bottom-up
solutions.idea: Fill best[i] left to right from the two base cases.

solutions.title: Two rolling variables
solutions.idea: Only the last two best values are ever read, so keep just those.

followups: Return the list of steps you stand on, not just the total.
Moves can be 1, 2 or 3 steps long. What changes?
